title: Cultivation of Cladophora glomerata Under Low‐Salinity Conditions: Ecological Controls, Production Constraints and Baltic Sea Deployment
content:
ABSTRACT

Brackish and freshwater coastal systems often combine nutrient enrichment with proximity to wastewater, aquaculture and coastal infrastructure, yet macroalgal cultivation under low-salinity conditions remains poorly validated. This review evaluates whether Cladophora glomerata, commonly managed as nuisance biomass, can be developed as a seasonal crop and nutrient-recovery tool in low-salinity systems, with emphasis on the Baltic Sea. A structured evidence synthesis used 80 sources selected from a broad evidence register, separating direct C. glomerata evidence from mechanistically transferable studies on Chaetomorpha, Rhizoclonium and other Cladophora species. The synthesis shows that salinity across the Baltic range is permissive rather than the dominant constraint: Observations indicate that Baltic material grows throughout the regional salinity gradient, whereas coastal lake populations persist near 5 psu and up to approximately 10 psu. Phosphorus sets carrying capacity, late-season nitrogen depletion reduces regrowth, high-pH boundary layers can restrict inorganic carbon access, self-shading confines photosynthesis to the canopy surface, weak renewal limits nutrient and carbon flux, and delayed harvest turns biomass into detrital nutrient recycling. Highest production and nutrient-removal benchmarks come mainly from nutrient-rich engineered systems and related filamentous green macroalgae, including production up to 24.3 t dry weight ha−1 year−1 and nutrient removal exceeding 85%. These values indicate design potential, not Baltic C. glomerata yield predictions. The main evidence gap is engineering and economics, not basic ecophysiology. Baltic trials should, therefore, test locally collected, vouchered and molecularly authenticated populations in thin, attached and repeatedly harvested canopies while measuring attachment stability, harvest interval, cumulative yield, nutrient recovery, dewatering, biomass quality, labour, energy demand and operating cost. C. glomerata is physiologically feasible under low salinity, but field-scale readiness remains unproven.
